solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

flags: minor: distractors A and D are directly contradicted by paragraph 4 and C invents a cause (lateness); few students would pick them, so the item is easy for a main-idea question
R037-01.notes: Last paragraph: noon went from a fact about the sky to an agreement; the railroads drove this. A and D contradict the 1918/'no act of Congress' point; C is not the passage's cause.

R037-02.notes: Sun moves westward; Boston (east) before New York before Chicago, so a town farther west reaches noon later still. One-step application of a stated pattern. A is the reversal trap.

flags: minor: B and D are implausible; C contradicts the timing (the clocks were before 1883)
R037-03.notes: Clocks 'each correct for some line and none correct for the street' illustrate the confusion from each railroad keeping its own time.

flags: minor: key closely paraphrases 'trains running in opposite directions had to meet and pass at sidings'; 'at set times' is a small, reasonable inference
R037-04.notes: Opposing trains on a single track must meet at sidings; mismatched clocks could put them on the same track at the same time.

flags: minor: key is a near-verbatim paraphrase of the paragraph 3 sentence (lookup item); B is the direction-reversal trap
R037-05.notes: Towns east of their zone's central meridian had already passed local noon, clocks were turned back, and noon came again. Historical facts check out: Nov 18, 1883 was a Sunday; the General Time Convention; four zones; telegraph time signals; 1918 Standard Time Act.

flags: Key wording is awkward and grammatically unlike the other choices: 'granting their legal point but not that it explained the change' has no attitude adjective and its 'it' is unclear (the objectors never claimed their point explained the change). Suggest e.g. 'qualified agreement, because they were right about the law but missed why the change succeeded.'
minor: answer cue: D is the only measured, two-sided choice; A, B and C are extreme or plainly contradicted ('They were, in a sense, correct')
R037-06.notes: The author concedes the objectors were 'in a sense, correct' (no legal authority) but says the railroads had something more effective, a network everyone needed. That is partial agreement.

R037-07.notes: 'What is striking is who made the change' = what is notable or remarkable. A ('forceful') is the literal-sense trap; B is the 'striking looks' sense.

flags: minor: C (disagreeing station clocks) is a tempting trap because it also shows clock time detached from the sun, but it illustrates the pre-1883 problem, not noon as a shared agreement
R037-08.notes: Under standard time, noon is a convention: the clocks can read noon although the sun is not yet highest, as happens west of a zone's meridian. A is the old sky-based noon; D reverses the change; C is the problem before standardization. Applying the idea to a new case adds a step.

flags: minor: overlaps somewhat with R037-01 (both test 'no act of Congress / spread by practice'); R037-01's choice D and this item's choice C are similar distractors
R037-09.notes: The 35-year gap between the 1883 adoption and the 1918 law supports the point that the change came by practice and the railroads' network, not by law. B, C and D are unsupported (C contradicts 'many cities adjusted within weeks').
